definitions.name: Exact response-type hypergeometric kernel
definitions.construction: \[K_N(x,y)=\binom{n}{m}^{-1}\!\!\sum_{\substack{0\le t_a\le a,\,0\le t_p\le p,\,0\le t_q\le q,\,0\le t_b\le b\\t_a+t_p+t_q+t_b=m,\,t_p+t_b=x\\q+b-t_q-t_b=y}}\binom a{t_a}\binom p{t_p}\binom q{t_q}\binom b{t_b}.\]

definitions.name: Finite squared-loss prior dual
definitions.construction: \[\mathcal B_{\mathsf D}(\pi)=\sum_{N\in\mathcal N_n}\pi_N\tau_N^2-\sum_{d:A_d^{\pi}>0}\frac{(B_d^{\pi})^2}{A_d^{\pi}},\qquad A_d^{\pi}=\sum_N\pi_N\Pr_N(\mathsf D=d),\quad B_d^{\pi}=\sum_N\pi_N\Pr_N(\mathsf D=d)\tau_N.\]

definitions.name: Active-gradient persistence handle
definitions.construction: Starting from the exact kernel \(K_N(x,y)\), determine the active states of a difference-only minimax rule at each even \(n\), form their full-cell risk gradients, and seek a legal state-prior mixture or a common strictly decreasing full-count perturbation on every active state. Use the exact \(00\)-plus-\(11\) padding recurrence only after controlling the three induced allocation sizes and all newly feasible response-type states.

definitions.name: Conditional boundary-layer handle
definitions.construction: Retain the bivariate hypergeometric likelihood before projecting to \(W\), derive the local without-replacement likelihood and Stein expansion on the least-favorable boundary layer, and compare the resulting bivariate variational problem with its one-dimensional projection to identify the first nonzero scale of \(\Delta_n\).

statements.statement: Under balanced complete randomization, averaging over unit permutations loses no minimax value, the observed-data orbit is exactly \((X_1,X_0)\), and its law at state \(N\) is \(K_N(x,y)\). Clipping and conditional expectation reduce attention to deterministic actions in \([-1,1]\). Consequently the two minimax values are exactly the games in Definitions 2 and 3, both minima are attained, \(\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}\le\rho_n^W\), and finite minimax duality gives \(\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}=\max_{\pi}\mathcal B_{(X_1,X_0)}(\pi)\) and \(\rho_n^W=\max_{\pi}\mathcal B_W(\pi)\).
statements.justification: This reduction makes every finite certificate a transparent randomization-game calculation from the four response types.
statements.gap: Ding and Dasgupta give the response-type table, while Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen give finite minimax duality for a different shifted-binomial experiment; neither states these two fixed-half games.
statements.consumer: Exact-balance software can evaluate an arbitrary full-count rule and a difference-only rule against the same finite schedule space.

statements.statement: The certificates \((g_2,\pi_2)\) and \((g_4,\pi_4)\) are primal-dual saddles for both observation maps. In particular, \[\rho_2^{\mathrm{CR}}=\rho_2^W=\frac14,\qquad \rho_4^{\mathrm{CR}}=\rho_4^W=1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.\] Every response-type state outside the displayed prior supports has risk strictly below the corresponding saddle value under the displayed rule.
statements.justification: The two smallest admissible populations establish that posterior relevance of the second count does not by itself imply minimax value.
statements.gap: No located complete-randomization minimax paper reports unrestricted full-count and difference-only equality at these exact finite sizes.
statements.consumer: The result provides regression tests for exact minimax implementations at the two smallest balanced sample sizes.

statements.statement: The map \(F_6\) has a unique zero \(s_6\) in the stated rational interval; all four weights \(A_6B_6\), \(B_6\), \(C_6B_6\), and \(D_6B_6\) are positive. The seven-state prior \(\pi_6\) makes \(g_6(W)\) the full-count posterior mean on every cell of positive predictive mass. The seven support-state risks equal \(s_6^2\), and each of the other \(77\) states has risk strictly below \(s_6^2\). Hence \[\rho_6^{\mathrm{CR}}=\rho_6^W=s_6^2.\]
statements.justification: The algebraic seven-state saddle is the nontrivial equality certificate needed to make eight the first failure rather than merely an example of failure.
statements.gap: Hull reports numerical complete-randomization evidence and Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen solve an independent-assignment scalar game; neither supplies this hypergeometric saddle or its \(77\) inactive inequalities.
statements.consumer: Finite-game solvers gain an exact algebraic benchmark that detects false strictness caused by arbitrary actions on prior-null cells.

statements.statement: The full-count rule \(t_8\) has maximum risk \(U_8\) over all \(165\) response-type states, with equality only at \((2,0,0,6)\) and \((6,0,0,2)\). The weights defining \(\pi_8^W\) are positive and sum to one, and its Bayes risk after observing \(W\) is \(L_8\). Exact rational comparison yields \[\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}\le U_8=\frac{457801172643}{7000000000000}<\frac{6541}{100000}<\frac{6578}{100000}<\frac{224641744872980943629642927781}{3414537001722982784239360000000}=L_8\le\rho_8^W.\] Therefore \(\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}<\rho_8^W\).
statements.justification: A separated rational primal-dual sandwich proves strict information value without relying on tolerances or an unattained numerical optimizer.
statements.gap: Blackwell garbling yields only weak dominance, and Hull's unrestricted-estimator complete-randomization discussion remains numerical and compares designs rather than the two analyses of one fixed design.
statements.consumer: Users of \(\operatorname{complete\_ra}\) with \(N=8\) learn that retaining both success counts can strictly lower worst-schedule MSE.

statements.statement: For each equality certificate at \(n=2,4,6\), the full-count posterior mean under the least-favorable prior is constant on every positive-predictive-mass \(W\)-fiber, and a scalar completion controls every remaining state. At \(n=8\), the certified full rule is not constant on the fiber \(W=2\), since \(t_8(1,0)=73084/10^6\) and \(t_8(2,1)=152579/10^6\), while Theorem 4 places its full-count worst risk below a lower bound valid for every \(W\)-rule. Thus the second count first changes the minimax envelope through failure of the scalar saddle equations, not through ordinary posterior relevance alone.
statements.justification: The proposition isolates the decision-theoretic mechanism behind the first strict threshold.
statements.gap: Blackwell's experiment order does not characterize equality for one target and one loss, while the published minimax papers do not inspect these fixed-half posterior fibers.
statements.consumer: Analysts can distinguish a statistic that is posterior-informative from one whose discarded information actually changes worst-case optimal risk.

statements.statement: Among all admissible positive even population sizes not exceeding eight, the equality set is exactly \(\{2,4,6\}\), and \(n=8\) is the first size at which compressing \((X_1,X_0)\) to \(W\) is minimax-lossy for ATE squared error.
statements.justification: This is the finite threshold result that turns four isolated calculations into one interpretable theorem.
statements.gap: The closest papers leave unrestricted complete-randomization behavior unresolved and do not identify a first sample-size cutoff for count compression.
statements.consumer: DeclareDesign users receive the first exact sample size at which the conventional count difference ceases to be a minimax-preserving data reduction.

statements.statement: Does \(\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}<\rho_n^W\) hold for every even \(n\ge10\)? Derive either a legal all-size family of full-count perturbations and matching active-state inequalities, or an explicit later even counterexample with a scalar saddle certificate. The derivation must control every new response-type state and cannot infer persistence from the \(n=8\) witness alone.
statements.justification: Strictness need not propagate because padding changes allocation mixtures, the feasible state lattice, and least-favorable supports.
statements.gap: Hull states a related general complete-randomization conjecture, while no located source gives the required uniform separating-prior or active-gradient argument for this compression comparison.
statements.consumer: A resolution would determine whether software should preserve the second count at every larger balanced binary experiment or only at selected sizes.

statements.statement: Determine the first nonzero normalization, leading limit or complete subsequential-limit set of \(\Delta_n\) along even \(n\), and decide whether \(\Delta_n=o(n^{-4/3})\). The construction must derive the two-coordinate hypergeometric boundary expansion before projecting to \(W\); no power law, constant, or parity law is prespecified.
statements.justification: The finite threshold does not reveal the asymptotic price of count compression, which may live below the common second-order minimax scale.
statements.gap: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen derive the Airy correction for a shifted-binomial experiment; finite-population central limit theory does not resolve the finer bivariate-versus-projected decision risk.
statements.consumer: A sharp scale would tell designers whether the finite information loss is practically persistent or asymptotically negligible relative to nonlinear shrinkage gains.

sampling_model.design: Uniform assignment over \(\mathcal Z_n\), the assignments treating exactly \(m=n/2\) units.
sampling_model.units: The \(n\) labeled units and both binary potential outcomes are fixed; the assignment is the only randomness.
sampling_model.treatment: One binary treatment with exactly \(m\) treated and \(m\) controls.
sampling_model.overlap: Every labeled exactly balanced assignment has probability \(1/\binom n m\).
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: There is no stochastic nuisance estimation; nature ranges over the finite response-type state space \(\mathcal N_n\).

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: ``Independent random assignment remains optimal, and the generally-nonlinear optimal estimator can meaningfully reduce worst-case MSE.''
``For binary potential outcomes, we show this minimax risk is equivalent to the minimax risk of an estimation problem with \(2\) unknown parameters.''
``A new proof of this result is given, and the restriction to experiments with a finite number of outcomes is removed.''
``This paper shows the minimax optimality of the complete randomization scheme under permutation invariance.''

tldr: Exact balance removes treatment-share variation but leaves two observed arm-success counts. For fixed binary potential outcomes, the full pair and its difference have the same worst-schedule ATE squared-error minimax risk at \(n=2,4,6\), including a seven-state algebraic saddle at six, but they separate at \(n=8\). A rational full-count rule and a rational difference-only prior certify \(\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}<0.06541<0.06578<\rho_8^W\), so eight is the first size at which the second count has minimax value. Later-size persistence and every asymptotic law for the compression tax remain open.

project_justification.gap: Published minimax analyses either optimize unrestricted assignment through a shifted-binomial reduction or study complete randomization with affine or prescribed estimators. Exact binary randomization-inference papers retain the observed table but do not compare unrestricted point-estimation risk with the risk after compressing it to the difference.
project_justification.niche: The fixed-half response-type hypergeometric experiment is a finite decision problem in which Blackwell weak dominance is automatic, yet strict value for ATE squared loss depends on the least-favorable posterior geometry.
project_justification.fill: The project gives analytic primal and least-favorable-prior equality certificates at \(n=2,4,6\), a complete algebraic verification at six, and a serialized rational upper-lower separation at eight, thereby locating the first exact failure of the scalar reduction.

related_work: Hull (2026, Theorem 1, Proposition 2, and footnote 12) shows that bounded outcomes can reverse familiar design prescriptions, proves complete-randomization suboptimality for an affine class, and leaves general-estimator complete-randomization strictness conjectural; it motivates but does not subsume the within-design count-compression question here. Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026, Theorems 2.1--2.2 and 3.1) reduce the unrestricted binary design-estimator game to a shifted-binomial experiment and derive nonlinear shrinkage and the Airy correction; their first changed proof step under fixed-half assignment is the independent scalar likelihood, which becomes the bivariate response-type hypergeometric kernel. Ding and Dasgupta (2016, Table 1, equation (1), and Section 2) supply the four response types and the observed two-by-two table used to derive that kernel. Blackwell (1953) implies that the full count pair weakly dominates its deterministic compression, but not that the inequality is strict for this one estimand and loss. Bai (2023, Theorems 3.1--3.3) establishes complete-randomization and Neyman-allocation results in a permutation-invariant linear framework, leaving arbitrary nonlinear rules over fixed binary schedules outside its scope. Rigdon and Hudgens (2015) and Li and Ding (2016) use the full binary table for exact confidence sets; they neither study minimax point estimation nor license a confidence-set claim here. Li and Ding (2017) provide first-order finite-population limit tools, not the finite threshold or higher-order information loss.
technical_internal_limitation: A prior can make the second count strictly Bayes-informative at \(n=4\) and \(n=6\) even though the minimax values are equal. Thus posterior relevance under an arbitrary prior cannot prove strict minimax separation. The \(n=8\) action is only a feasible full-count upper certificate, and the \(n=8\) prior is only a difference-game lower certificate; neither exact minimax value at eight is claimed.
honest_scope: The finite response-type games, equality at \(n=2,4,6\), strict separation at \(n=8\), and the first-lossy-size conclusion are theorem-level targets. The paper makes no confidence-set claim, no pointwise-dominance claim, and no assertion that \(t_8\) is exact minimax. Strictness for any even \(n\ge10\), every power law or constant for \(\Delta_n\), parity-dependent limits, and all higher-order balance-tax statements remain open. The standard special-case check is exact: at \(n=2\), both experiments reduce to the displayed three-state saddle with value \(1/4\).
